props.title: The End of Summer

sections.content: Yasujiro Ozu's The End of Summer (1961) represents one of his final masterpieces, completing his meditation on family dissolution and generational change in post-war Japan. Like his earlier Tokyo Story (1953) and Late Spring (1949), Ozu employs his distinctive low-angle shots and contemplative pacing to examine how traditional family structures crack under modernization's pressure. The story of the Kohayagawa family's sake brewery and their patriarch's last summer becomes a lens through which Ozu captures the bittersweet transformation of Japanese society.

sections.content: What sets The End of Summer apart is its unique balance of comedy and melancholy. Unlike the more overtly dramatic Floating Weeds (1959), Ozu infuses genuine humor into the family dynamics, particularly through Ganjiro Nakamura's performance as the mischievous patriarch Manbei. His secret meetings with an old flame provide both comic relief and deeper commentary on the clash between personal desire and family obligation - a theme Ozu would revisit in his final work An Autumn Afternoon (1962).

The film's visual composition reflects Ozu's mature style at its peak. Like Early Summer (1951), he uses careful framing and his famous "pillow shots" of empty spaces to create emotional resonance. The sake brewery becomes a character itself, its traditional architecture standing in stark contrast to the modern offices and apartments that represent Japan's economic miracle. These visual motifs would influence later directors like Hirokazu Kore-eda, particularly in Still Walking (2008). SUBHEAD: The Evolution of Family Drama in Japanese Cinema

sections.content: The End of Summer bridges classic Japanese family drama with emerging modern sensibilities. While contemporaries like Akira Kurosawa were making dynamic samurai epics like Yojimbo (1961), Ozu maintained his focus on domestic life but incorporated subtle references to Japan's rapid westernization. This approach would influence later family dramas like Kon Ichikawa's The Makioka Sisters (1983) and Yoji Yamada's Tokyo Family (2013), a direct homage to Ozu's style.
